processes: Conducting heat and electricity via free-moving electrons
Being hammered into sheets and drawn into wires
Losing electrons to form positive ions
plainLanguageExplanation: A metal is an element with a set of signature properties you can see and feel. Metals are shiny — think of polished gold or aluminum foil. They are malleable, meaning they can be hammered into thin sheets, and ductile, meaning they can be drawn into wires. Most importantly, metals are excellent conductors of heat and electricity — which is why your house's electrical wires and cooking pans are made of metal. These properties come from how metal atoms behave: their outer electrons are loose and free to wander between atoms, which lets electricity flow and heat travel easily. About 80% of the elements are metals. They fill the left side and the middle of the periodic table, from the alkali metals in Group 1 through the transition metals in the center, like iron, copper, and gold. In reactions, metals tend to give away their loose outer electrons, becoming positive ions — which is why metals like sodium and iron pair up with nonmetals to form ionic compounds.

whyItMatters: Metals built the modern world — the copper in your electronics, the steel in bridges, the aluminum in cans, the gold in jewelry. Their loose-electron structure is also a doorway into understanding how electricity flows, how ionic bonds form, and why so much of the periodic table shares a family resemblance.
didYouKnow: The most common metal in Earth's crust isn't iron — it's aluminum, and it is everywhere from soda cans to airplane bodies.
compareReason: Metals and nonmetals are opposites in look, feel, conduction, and position on the table — comparing them makes both families' defining traits unmistakable.
